23b09478a589: Acceptance Was the Answer: The Big Book's Page 417 Passage
f030f592a5e3: What the most-quoted passage in the Big Book teaches about serenity, and where acceptance ends and action begins
9b814e244533: The passage almost everyone is looking for sits on page 417 of <0>Alcoholics Anonymous</0>, 4th Edition, in a personal story called <1>Acceptance Was the Answer</1>. The writer, a physician who was addicted to both alcohol and pills, opens the most-quoted paragraph in the book by telling us that 'acceptance is the answer to all my problems today' (page 417). When he is disturbed, he says, it is because he finds 'some person, place, thing, or situation' unacceptable to him, and he can find no serenity until he accepts that person, place, thing, or situation as being 'exactly the way it is supposed to be at this moment' (page 417).
5bd54f5099ac: If the page number looks wrong to you, you may be remembering an older printing. In the 3rd Edition this same story was titled <0>Doctor, Alcoholic, Addict</0>, and the acceptance passage fell on page 449. When the 4th Edition came out in 2001, the story was renamed and the book repaged, so the words we heard quoted as 'page 449' now live on page 417.
a1993a2240ea: The paragraph makes a claim big enough to argue with: 'Nothing, absolutely nothing, happens in God's world by mistake' (page 417). The doctor is not saying that everything that happens is good. He is saying that serenity begins when we stop demanding that reality be different than it is right now. He tells us he had to accept his own alcoholism before he could ever stay sober, and that 'unless I accept life completely on life's terms, I cannot be happy' (page 417). Then he turns the lens all the way around: he needed to concentrate less on what needed changing in the world and more on what needed changing in himself and his attitudes (page 417). That is the hinge of the whole passage. His hard experience distills into one line many of us keep taped to the mirror: 'When I stopped living in the problem and began living in the answer, the problem went away' (page 417).
7b6931f6b375: <0>Acceptance is not approval.</0> It does not mean we like what happened, that we excuse cruelty, or that we stay quietly in situations that harm us. It means we stop burning our strength in a war with facts. The basic text asks the same surrender of us about our drinking: 'We learned that we had to fully concede to our innermost selves that we were alcoholics' (page 30). We could not recover from a condition we refused to admit we had. The same spirit shows up in the promises that follow Step Ten: 'And we have ceased fighting anything or anyone—even alcohol' (page 84). Ceasing to fight is not quitting on life. It is how we finally join it.
88afcdeb275d: Neither is acceptance a permission slip for passivity. The same book that gives us page 417 sends us out the door to make our amends (page 76) and to sweep off our side of the street (page 77), and it tells us plainly that 'Helping others is the foundation stone of your recovery' (page 97). Acceptance is where action becomes possible. We accept what we cannot change so that we have the strength to change what we can, starting with ourselves.
d39422fb7006: A Story, Not a Set of Instructions
a30f01213615: It helps to know where these words live. Page 417 sits in the personal stories section of the Big Book, not in the first 164 pages that lay out the program of recovery. That does not make the passage less true. It makes it testimony. A physician is telling us what actually kept him sober, one day at a time. The stories exist to show us the principles walking around in real lives, and this one is quoted by page number in meetings all over the world. The basic text and the story agree completely: we admit what is, we turn over what we cannot manage, and we get to work on what we can.
4f4565ec105b: So how do we use it? The next time we are disturbed, we can try the doctor's inventory. What person, place, thing, or situation are we refusing to accept? Then comes a second question: what part of this is actually ours to change? Usually the honest answer is our own attitude and our own next action, exactly as page 417 suggests. The Big Book reminds us that what we really have is 'a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition' (page 85), and acceptance is part of each day's maintenance. We do not have to accept forever, only for today. We do not have to like it, only to stop fighting it. Serenity waits on the other side of that surrender.

08c6a4f15fbe: What pages 76 to 84 ask of us, and what they promise in return
54f56bbb5ec1: The Big Book covers making amends on pages 76 through 84, in the chapter called Into Action. Step Eight asks us to list everyone we have harmed and become willing to make amends to them all. Step Nine asks us to make 'direct amends to such people wherever possible, except when to do so would injure them or others' (page 59). The book spends barely a paragraph on Step Eight, and the reason is practical: we already made the list when we took our inventory (page 76). What remains is willingness, and the book tells us that if we do not have it yet, we keep asking until it comes.
bac7fc2817c9: Why do we do it at all? Page 76 opens this stretch of the book by reminding us that 'Faith without works is dead.' The spiritual experience we found in the earlier steps has to be carried into our relationships or it withers. Page 77 gives the purpose in a single sentence: 'Our real purpose is to fit ourselves to be of maximum service to God and the people about us.' We are not making amends mainly to feel better or to be forgiven. We are sweeping away the wreckage of self-will so we can be useful again.
eace2c615a59: What Direct Amends Actually Look Like
ddf99b10bccd: Direct means we go to the person, face to face wherever possible, rather than sending a vague apology from a safe distance. The book walks through real situations. We approach the person we have resented or wronged 'in a helpful and forgiving spirit' (page 77), keeping the focus on our own side of the street; his faults are not our business that day. With creditors, page 78 says we do not dodge them. We let them know we are sorry and arrange the best repayment we can. Even wrongs that could cost us our reputation or worse are on the table. Page 79 sets the standard plainly: 'We must not shrink at anything.' We ask God for strength and direction to do the right thing, whatever the personal consequences may be.
6a62f790068a: Step Nine carries one careful exception: we make amends except when doing so would injure the person or somebody else. Notice what the clause does not say. It does not say except when it is embarrassing, expensive, or frightening for us. The injury in question is theirs, never ours. Page 79 warns that we are not to be 'the hasty and foolish martyr' who needlessly sacrifices others to save himself. Buying our own peace of mind at another person's expense is not an amend; it is one more act of selfishness wearing Step Nine clothing. The book's examples on pages 80 and 81 involve confessions that would wound a spouse or pull innocent people into harm. In those cases we seek guidance first, talking things over with others and asking God for direction before taking any drastic step (page 80). The willingness stays total. The method stays considerate.
4cd9a0578585: Page 82 gives the most vivid picture in the book of why an apology is not enough: 'The alcoholic is like a tornado roaring his way through the lives of others.' A tornado cannot fix a town by saying sorry to it. Speaking of the family, page 83 is blunt: 'A remorseful mumbling that we are sorry won't fill the bill at all.' What fills the bill is repair. We pay what we owe, we tell the truth we withheld, and above all we live differently at home, day after day, so the people closest to us experience the change instead of just hearing about it. The book is also honest that some wrongs can never be fully righted. Page 83 says we do not worry about those if we can honestly say we would right them if we could. Willingness is the coin of this step.
b8eff2740bfc: Right in the middle of the Step Nine instructions, the book pauses to tell us what happens if we do this work thoroughly. 'If we are painstaking about this phase of our development, we will be amazed before we are half way through' (page 83). Then come the Ninth Step Promises: 'We are going to know a new freedom and a new happiness. We will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' (page 83). Fear of people, self-pity, and the old feeling of uselessness begin to slip away as the amends get made. Page 84 closes the passage with the assurance generations of us have tested: 'They will always materialize if we work for them.' We do not have to finish the list this week. We simply have to start, stay willing, and keep walking toward the next name.

e75702feed30: Why the Big Book says helping another alcoholic is the surest way to stay sober ourselves
75709bc4de19: Carrying the message is the heart of Step 12: <0>"Having had a spiritual awakening as the result of these steps, we tried to carry this message to alcoholics, and to practice these principles in all our affairs"</0> (page 60). The Big Book devotes an entire chapter to it, Chapter 7, Working With Others, and opens with one of the most quoted lines in the whole book: "Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics" (page 89). Notice what that sentence actually claims. Not that helping others is a nice extra once we feel better, but that it protects our own sobriety more reliably than anything else we can do.
986fb792b4f5: The same page makes it a direct instruction: "Carry this message to other alcoholics!" (page 89). Then it tells us why we, of all people, are qualified: "You can help when no one else can" (page 89). Doctors, family, and friends may have tried for years to reach a drinker and failed. But one alcoholic talking honestly to another gets a hearing nobody else gets, because we have been where they are. Our drinking history, the thing we were most ashamed of, becomes the very credential that lets us reach someone still suffering.
6dfa0beeab65: Why Working With Others Keeps Us Sober
e95296d14ac9: The Big Book is blunt about our stake in this. Early in the book it says "our very lives, as ex-problem drinkers, depend upon our constant thought of others and how we may help meet their needs" (page 20). That is strong language, and it is meant to be. The alcoholic mind drifts back toward self, and self-centeredness is described on page 62 as the root of our troubles. Twelfth Step work is the practical antidote. When we sit with a newcomer, we cannot stay wrapped up in our own problems. We hear our own story out of someone else's mouth, and we remember exactly what we were saved from.
bd9e199c2f00: Chapter 7 also promises something beyond protection. "Life will take on new meaning" (page 89). Watching people recover, watching them turn around and help others, watching a fellowship grow up around us, the book says this is an experience we must not miss. Later in the chapter it goes further still: "Helping others is the foundation stone of your recovery" (page 97), and it adds that an occasional kindly act is not enough. This is daily material, not a merit badge we earn once.
77b477d67377: How We Actually Carry the Message
5264027d7324: The chapter is practical about method. We are told to learn what we can about the prospect first, to approach him when he is ready to listen rather than when he is very drunk, and to talk as one alcoholic to another, sharing our own drinking history before we ever mention a solution (pages 90-91). We describe ourselves as someone who has found an answer, not as someone recruiting for a cause. If he is not interested, we do not force it; the book tells us not to waste time chasing a man who cannot or will not work with us, because our job is to be useful, not to argue anyone into recovery (page 96). And carrying the message is bigger than formal Twelfth Step calls. It is sponsorship, greeting the newcomer at a meeting, sharing honestly, and letting our changed life speak. The book's closing page puts it simply: "Give freely of what you find and join us" (page 164).
2e4163e1e738: Step 12 begins with a condition: having had a spiritual awakening <0>as the result of these steps</0>. We carry a message we have actually received. That is why the first eleven steps matter so much; without them we have sympathy to offer, but not a solution. The awakening does not need to be dramatic. Appendix II describes most of our spiritual experiences as gradual, of the educational variety (pages 567-568). What matters is that something real has changed in us, and we give it away to keep it. Freely we received, so freely we give. That exchange, one alcoholic helping another, is the engine that has kept this fellowship alive since two men sat down together in Akron in 1935.

eeb39f712029: Big Book page 85 says we have a daily reprieve contingent on our spiritual condition. Here is what that maintenance looks like in Steps Ten and Eleven.

f1a72850c106: The Daily Reprieve on Page 85 of the Big Book
47223a3edf35: What maintaining our spiritual condition actually looks like, one day at a time
f51b435a972c: The words people remember are on page 85 of Alcoholics Anonymous, in the chapter called Into Action: 'What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition' (page 85). In plain language, sobriety is not a prize we win once and keep forever. It is renewed one day at a time, and it holds only as long as we keep doing the spiritual work that produced it. Two sentences earlier the book is blunt: 'We are not cured of alcoholism' (page 85). A reprieve is not a pardon. It is a stay, granted for today.
4d0fd5e19826: So what is the maintenance the reprieve depends on? The book does not leave us guessing. That sentence sits in the middle of the instructions for Steps Ten and Eleven (pages 84-88). Maintenance means a personal inventory that runs all day, mistakes set right quickly, and prayer and meditation in the morning, at night, and whenever we get rattled in between. The sections below walk through it straight from the text.
7dbcf357366f: What Page 85 Is Warning Us About
280a60c5b45f: Just before the famous line, the book describes how good recovered life can feel. The problem has been removed. We are not fighting liquor or even avoiding temptation, and we feel as if we had been placed in 'a position of neutrality—safe and protected' (page 85). That new attitude toward liquor arrives without any thought or effort on our part (page 85). Then comes the warning: 'It is easy to let up on the spiritual program of action and rest on our laurels. We are headed for trouble if we do, for alcohol is a subtle foe' (page 85). The threat is not that the program stops working. The threat is that we stop working the program because it worked. The neutrality lasts, the book says, 'so long as we keep in fit spiritual condition' (page 85).
6332bf144226: Step Ten: The Inventory That Never Stops
aa1654b59b18: Maintenance begins on page 84 with Step Ten, which asks us to keep taking personal inventory and to set right new mistakes as we go along (page 84). The instruction is concrete: 'Continue to watch for selfishness, dishonesty, resentment, and fear' (page 84). When these crop up, we ask God at once to remove them, talk them over with someone, and make amends quickly if we have harmed anyone, then turn our thoughts to someone we can help (page 84). This is not a yearly housecleaning. It is a spot-check we run in the middle of ordinary days, and the book says it should continue for our lifetime (page 84). The attitude behind it fits in seven words: 'Love and tolerance of others is our code' (page 84).
6523e58baec3: Step Eleven: Morning, Night, and All Through the Day
67d8b3aacc14: Page 85 then turns to Step Eleven, prayer and meditation, and pages 86 through 88 lay out a rhythm anyone can follow. At night: 'When we retire at night, we constructively review our day. Were we resentful, selfish, dishonest or afraid?' (page 86). After the review we ask God's forgiveness and what corrective measures should be taken, careful not to slide into worry or morbid reflection (page 86). In the morning: 'On awakening let us think about the twenty-four hours ahead' (page 86), asking God to direct our thinking before the day starts. And in the thick of things: 'As we go through the day we pause, when agitated or doubtful, and ask for the right thought or action' (page 87), reminding ourselves that we are no longer running the show (pages 87-88). The book closes these instructions with a plain reassurance: 'It works—it really does' (page 88).
4c2368426200: Why a Daily Reprieve Is Good News
d62769d541cb: At first, contingent sobriety can sound like living under a suspended sentence. Read it again and it turns into freedom. We are not asked to stay sober forever. We are asked to maintain our spiritual condition today, and 'Every day is a day when we must carry the vision of God's will into all of our activities' (page 85). The book even calls this kind of effort the proper use of the will (page 85), so we are not passive in it. The maintenance is not a tax added on top of sobriety. It is the same set of actions that made us well, kept warm. Yes, the reprieve is contingent. It is also renewable every single morning, for as long as we are willing to do the simple things pages 84 through 88 describe. We do not have to be cured. We have something that works one day at a time, and today is the only day we are asked to work it.

ecb6d659b2a3: How the Big Book has us review our fears — and what it offers in their place.
3f08f51aae93: The Big Book's fear inventory lives on pages 67 and 68, in Chapter 5, How It Works — a few short paragraphs tucked between the resentment inventory and the review of our relationships. Short, but not small. The book introduces fear with unusual force: 'It was an evil and corroding thread; the fabric of our existence was shot through with it' (page 67). If you have ever gotten honest about what actually drove the drinking — and the lying, the hiding, the big talk — you know why the book gives fear its own review.
832f8ae41696: The directions are plainer than we expect. 'We reviewed our fears thoroughly. We put them on paper, even though we had no resentment in connection with them' (page 68). That last clause matters. In the resentment inventory we had already noticed fear sitting underneath entry after entry. Here the book has us list the fears that stand on their own — fear of losing a job, a marriage, our health, our standing, fear of being found out, fear of ending up alone. On paper, each one, by name. Fear does its best work in the dark, and the inventory is simply the act of turning the lights on.
6af6e613a9ed: Then comes the question that turns a list into an inventory: 'We asked ourselves why we had them. Wasn't it because self-reliance failed us?' (page 68). We had run our lives on our own strength, our own cleverness, our own plans — and the returns kept shrinking. Self-reliance was the strategy, and fear was the receipt. The book allows that self-reliance was good as far as it went, but it didn't go far enough. When the bet is everything and the bankroll is only ourselves, fear is simply honest arithmetic.
b0ec6f5f13b8: The fear inventory doesn't end with insight; it ends with a change of ground. 'We are now on a different basis; the basis of trusting and relying upon God' (page 68). Instead of demanding that we be big enough for every threat, we hand the outcome to something bigger than us. The practical prayer is right there in the text: 'We ask Him to remove our fear and direct our attention to what He would have us be' (page 68). Notice the direction of that prayer — not toward the thing we're afraid of losing, but toward who we might become. And the book's promise for this piece of work is immediate and modest: 'At once, we commence to outgrow fear' (page 68). Commence. It is a beginning renewed daily, not a lightning cure.
f0c967c2d6ff: If you are on Step Four, take a fresh sheet and write down every fear you can name, whether or not it connects to a resentment. Beside each one, ask the book's question: why do I have it? Where did relying on myself alone actually leave me? Then use the prayer on page 68 for each fear on the list, and bring the whole sheet to your sponsor when you share your Fifth Step. Many of us date the real loosening of fear's grip to that one honest conversation. The Promises even circle back to this work later in the book: 'Fear of people and of economic insecurity will leave us' (page 84). The old fears may still knock. The difference is that we no longer have to answer the door alone.

b948fc32f31f: The words we hear at almost every meeting: pages 58 to 60, taken slowly
a57ad266a66f: <0>How It Works</0> is the title of Chapter 5 of <1>Alcoholics Anonymous</1>, the Big Book, and the part most of us know by heart sits on pages 58 through 60. This is the passage read aloud at the start of almost every AA meeting. It opens with one of the most famous sentences in recovery: "Rarely have we seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path" (page 58). In three short pages the book hands us the whole program in miniature: honesty as the one requirement, willingness to go to any length, the Twelve Steps themselves, and three plain conclusions about our condition and where the help comes from.
603e0770c093: So how does it work? Through honesty and thoroughness. Page 58 says the people who do not recover are usually those who "cannot or will not completely give themselves to this simple program," people who are "constitutionally incapable of being honest with themselves" (page 58). Notice what that sentence does not say. It does not say we fail because we are too weak, too far gone, or too bad. The book puts the outcome in our hands: if we can get honest with ourselves and follow the path thoroughly, we recover.
bef9edeafdfa: The Promise and the Price on Page 58
31214e8e9328: Page 58 asks whether we want what sober members have and whether we are willing to go to any length to get it. Many of us balked at some of the Steps. "We thought we could find an easier, softer way. But we could not" (page 58). So the book pleads with us: "With all the earnestness at our command, we beg of you to be fearless and thorough from the very start" (page 58). Holding on to our old ideas got us nowhere until we let go absolutely. Then comes the reminder of the opponent: alcohol is "cunning, baffling, powerful" (pages 58 and 59), and without help it is too much for us. But there is One who has all power, and the book's whole hope for us fits in five words: "May you find Him now!" (page 59).
d0d2c89f02b0: Page 59 gives us the hinge of the chapter: "Half measures availed us nothing. We stood at the turning point. We asked His protection and care with complete abandon" (page 59). Most of us tried the half measures first. We cut down, switched drinks, made promises, worked a Step or two and skipped the uncomfortable ones. The turning point is the moment we admit our own plans have run out and give ourselves to the program completely. Right after that surrender the book says, "Here are the steps we took, which are suggested as a program of recovery" (page 59), and lists all Twelve Steps across pages 59 and 60. Suggested, not commanded. The book never bullies us; it simply reports what worked for the people who wrote it.
cdbf937692c4: After the Steps, the book gathers everything into three pertinent ideas, the ones we call the abc's (page 60): <0>(a)</0> "That we were alcoholic and could not manage our own lives," <1>(b)</1> "That probably no human power could have relieved our alcoholism," and <2>(c)</2> "That God could and would if He were sought" (page 60). The first is Step One in a single line. The second closes the exits we kept trying: willpower alone, the love of our families, our own best thinking. None of it relieved the illness by itself. The third is pure hope, and it is worth reading slowly. It does not say God might help us. It says He could and would, on one condition only: that He be sought.
12ddb016c61f: Page 60 also expects our panic. Many of us exclaimed, "What an order! I can't go through with it." The reply is gentle: "Do not be discouraged" (page 60). The book admits that "No one among us has been able to maintain anything like perfect adherence to these principles" (page 60). "We are not saints. The point is, that we are willing to grow along spiritual lines" (page 60). Then comes the sentence many of us lean on every day: "We claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection" (page 60). That is why these pages open our meetings. Not to scold us, but to remind us that the path is walkable. We show up honest, we take the Steps thoroughly, and we let God do for us what we could not do for ourselves.

71710ce8131c: The last page of the basic text promises that our understanding will keep growing
66d10ff4adcd: In recovery, 'more will be revealed' is shorthand for one of the most hopeful promises in the Big Book. It comes from page 164, the very last page of the basic text, where the first members wrote, 'Our book is meant to be suggestive only. We realize we know only a little. God will constantly disclose more to you and to us.' That is the whole idea in three plain sentences. The people who wrote the book were not handing us a finished system. They were handing us a beginning, and they promised that God would keep teaching all of us, writers and readers alike, as we walked forward.
3c4e89d604a6: The saying means two things at once. First, humility. Even the founders admitted they knew only a little, so none of us has to pretend we have it all figured out. Second, hope. Our understanding of God, of ourselves, and of this way of living is not stuck at today's level. If we stay sober and keep doing the work, more gets disclosed. The book calls itself suggestive rather than final (page 164), and that leaves room for every one of us to grow past where we started.
9f3ba8eb17f6: Here is a detail worth knowing: the exact words 'more will be revealed' do not appear anywhere in the Big Book. The fellowship condensed the page 164 promise into a saying, and it stuck because it names something we all experience. The passage sits in the closing paragraphs of the chapter <0>A Vision For You</0>, at the end of the basic text. Right after promising that God will constantly disclose more, the book gives us a job. It says, 'Ask Him in your morning meditation what you can do each day for the man who is still sick.' Then it adds, 'The answers will come, if your own house is in order.' Revelation and action travel together. We do not receive more light by sitting still. We receive it by praying, cleaning house, and helping the next alcoholic (page 164).
a5a8df3e25da: Calling the book suggestive was a deliberate act of humility, and it protects us from turning the program into a rigid rulebook. The same spirit shows up on page 60, where the book says, 'We claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection.' The Steps are offered there as guides to progress, and the book admits that no one among us has maintained anything like perfect adherence to these principles (page 60). If the founders could say they knew only a little, we can say it too. That admission keeps us teachable, and teachable people stay sober.
7e6faa3f7026: It also matters because our reprieve is daily. Page 85 reminds us that we are not cured of alcoholism; what we really have is 'a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition.' A daily reprieve calls for daily growth. If the book had claimed to be the final word, we might read it once and coast. Because it claims to be suggestive only, we keep coming back, to the text and to God, for the next lesson.
541737ccc909: How More Gets Revealed in Practice
43d837f2ff1c: The disclosure is gradual, and the book says so. Describing life after Step Ten, page 84 tells us our next function is to grow in understanding and effectiveness, and that 'This is not an overnight matter. It should continue for our lifetime.' We work the Steps, we pray and meditate, we keep our side of the street clean, and understanding arrives on God's schedule rather than ours. Most of us can see it when we look back. Page 100 says we realize that 'the things which came to us when we put ourselves in God's hands were better than anything we could have planned.'
24db4b4b2d8d: So when an old-timer smiles and says more will be revealed, they are not brushing us off. They are handing us the last page of the basic text, in spirit if not in letter. The God of our understanding is still teaching, the program we know today is not the ceiling, and our part is the willingness, honesty, and open-mindedness that Appendix II names as essentials (page 568). We show up for morning meditation, we keep our house in order, we give freely of what we find. The book closes by promising that 'you will surely meet some of us as you trudge the Road of Happy Destiny' (page 164). More will be revealed on that road. It always is.
